content: The article discusses the upcoming upgrade of the pneumococcal vaccine in Taiwan, scheduled for 2026, to effectively address serotype replacement caused by widespread childhood vaccination. Since the introduction of the PCV13 vaccine for children ten years ago, there has been a significant reduction in severe pneumococcal infections, particularly among children, and a corresponding indirect protective effect observed in elderly populations. However, as seen in the U.S. experience, the widespread use of childhood vaccines has led to serotype replacement—where non-vaccine serotypes become more prevalent. To combat this, advanced countries such as the U.S., Canada, and EU nations have adopted PCV20 and PCV21 as priority vaccines for older adults and high-risk groups. In Taiwan, the Ministry of Health and Welfare’s Infectious Disease Prevention Advisory Committee, in a meeting held in September 2025, decided that individuals aged 19 to 64 with high-risk conditions who have completed a PCV13/15 and PPV23 series before age 65 may receive a booster dose of PCV20 or PCV21 within five years. The article emphasizes that increasing pneumococcal vaccination rates, especially among high-risk groups, is critical to maintaining public health protection.

content: A new vaccine against 21 strains of pneumococcal disease is being developed in a joint international study. The study aims to provide greater protection for children against the common infection that causes pneumonia, otitis media, and meningitis. According to 'News medical life science', the study led by the Murdoch Children's Research Institute (MCRI) in Australia is evaluating a promising vaccine that protects against 21 strains of pneumococcal disease, compared to the current 13 strains included in the national immunization program. The Melbourne branch of the randomized controlled trial will test 50 families with healthy two-month-old children who have not received routine vaccinations. Participants will receive four doses of the vaccine at two months, four and a half months, and 12-15 months, in addition to all recommended childhood vaccinations in the national immunization plan (NIP). The study aims to enroll over 1600 children from Australia, the United States, Puerto Rico, Honduras, South Korea, and Thailand to ensure the vaccine's safety and ability to induce protective antibody responses in young children. Participants will be followed up for up to 19 months and will undergo three blood tests. Pneumococcal disease can cause severe illnesses and death in children under two years old. In 2024, 602 cases of invasive pneumococcal disease were reported in Victoria, including 373 cases among children aged 0-4 years. content: A clinical study by 'Merck' showed that the new pneumococcal vaccine Capvaxive elicits strong and effective immune responses in children and adolescents aged 2‑18 with chronic illnesses or immunodeficiency, outperforming the older PPSV23 vaccine. The study, which included participants up to 18 years old, demonstrated that Capvaxive covers a wide range of pneumococcal serotypes responsible for pneumonia, meningitis, and sepsis—diseases that pose a serious threat to vulnerable populations. Safety data indicated no serious adverse events during the trial, supporting the likelihood of future regulatory approval. Researchers suggest that incorporating Capvaxive into national immunization programs could markedly reduce respiratory disease burden, lower mortality, and decrease hospital admissions, especially in communities lacking robust health systems or facing high rates of antibiotic‑resistant bacterial infections.

content: Capbaxiv, a 21‑valent adult pneumococcal conjugate vaccine, has been approved by the Korean Ministry of Food and Drug Safety (MFDS) for use in adults aged 18 and older. The MFDS granted product‑licence on 27 August 2025 for the pre‑filled syringe formulation (source: article). The vaccine protects against 21 pneumococcal serotypes—3, 6A, 7F, 8, 9N, 10A, 11A, 12F, 15A, 15B, 15C, 16F, 17F, 19A, 20A, 22F, 23A, 23B, 24F, 31, 33F, 35B (source: article)—and is administered as a single 0.5 ml intramuscular injection (source: article). Capbaxiv was approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in June 2023 (source: article). The vaccine is specifically designed for adults; it covers serotypes responsible for about 84 % of pneumococcal disease in adults aged 50 and older, a higher coverage than existing conjugate vaccines (source: article). Compared with the 20‑valent Prevnar20 and the 15‑valent Bexovax, Capbaxiv includes eight unique serotypes (15A, 15C, 16F, 23A, 23B, 24F, 31, 35B) that address the main causes of invasive pneumococcal disease in adults (source: article). Pneumococcal disease remains a major public‑health issue: in Korea it was the third leading cause of death in 2021 and the leading cause of respiratory‑infection deaths (source: article), and globally it caused 740,000 deaths among children and adolescents in 2019 (source: article).

content: Japan has approved a 21‑valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV21) that targets the serotypes most responsible for invasive pneumococcal disease (IPD) in adults. The vaccine contains 21 serotypes—3, 6A, 7F, 8, 9N, 10A, 11A, 12F, 15A, 15B‑o‑deacetylated, 16F, 17F, 19A, 20A, 22F, 23A, 23B, 24F, 31, 33F, and 35B—linked to the carrier protein CRM197. It adds eight serotypes (15A, 15B‑o‑deacetylated, 16F, 23A, 23B, 24F, 31, 35B) that are not covered by existing PCVs, thereby broadening protection. Clinical trials—including the domestic phase III 009 study, the overseas phase III 003 study, and the international phase III 008 study—confirmed the vaccine’s efficacy and safety. As of June 2025, the vaccine is approved in seven countries or regions (the United States, Puerto Rico, Canada, Australia, the EU, the United Kingdom, and the UAE). Common adverse events reported are injection‑site pain (36.0 %), headache, and fatigue (each >10 %). Serious reactions such as shock or anaphylaxis are rare but possible. The vaccine is expected to provide wider protection against pneumococcal disease in adults compared with earlier PCVs. The article notes that "注射部位疼痛（36.0%）" and "頭痛、疲労（各10%以上）" are the main side‑effects, and that "ショック、アナフィラキシーの可能性がある" should be taken into account.

title: Grippesaison 2025: Grippe-Viren grassieren wieder - so schützen Sie sich richtig
content: The 2025-2026 influenza season has begun, and health experts recommend vaccination to prevent severe illness. Influenza is caused by influenza viruses transmitted via respiratory droplets or contact with contaminated surfaces. Symptoms include sudden onset of fever, sore throat, dry cough, and body aches, with potential complications such as pneumonia, especially in older adults and children. Unlike COVID-19, which has a longer incubation period, flu symptoms appear rapidly. Due to overlapping symptoms, a doctor’s consultation and a COVID-19 test are advised for accurate diagnosis. The Robert Koch Institute (RKI) recommends flu vaccination for individuals aged 60 and above, pregnant women from the second trimester (and from the first if they have comorbidities), people with chronic illnesses, immunocompromised individuals, residents of care facilities, and those with frequent public contact. While not universally recommended for healthy individuals under 60, anyone may get vaccinated. The flu vaccine offers partial protection, with effectiveness varying by season, virus type, and individual factors such as age or prior infection. Protection begins 10–14 days after vaccination. Side effects are generally mild and include fever, fatigue, muscle aches, and local reactions at the injection site. The live attenuated nasal vaccine (LAIV) is contraindicated in children with severe asthma, immunodeficiency, or salicylate therapy. Vaccination is not advised during acute illness or fever above 38°C. Simultaneous administration of flu and COVID-19 vaccines is permitted, with injections given in different limbs. No serious adverse effects have been reported in clinical trials. The Paul-Ehrlich-Institut provides updated information on vaccine strains for the 2025/26 season.

title: Vacina infantil contra pneumonia terá versão 'mais potente' no SUS a partir de 2026
content: Brazil’s National Immunization Program (PNI) announced that a new, more potent pneumococcal vaccine will be added to the SUS schedule in 2026. The current 10‑valent vaccine (Pncc10) protects against 10 serotypes and is given in three doses at 2, 4 and 12 months. Recent studies show that 264 invasive pneumococcal disease cases were reported in children ≤2 years in 2023‑24, and 92.3% of those cases in vaccinated children were caused by serotypes 19A and 3, indicating vaccine escape. PNI Director Éder Gatti said, 'Nos anos de 2023 e 2024, observamos 264 casos de doença pneumocócica invasiva em crianças de até 2 anos que tiveram oportunidade de se vacinar. Desse total, 92,3% dos casos em crianças vacinadas apenas com a Pncc10 foram provocados pelos sorotipos 19A e 3.' The new vaccine will cover these serotypes, and the government will adopt a flexible procurement strategy, allowing the PNI to switch between 13‑, 15‑, or 20‑valent formulations based on epidemiology. The new vaccine is expected to enter the national schedule in 2026, while families should continue the current schedule until then.
